name: Clinical strength antiperspirant
lead: Clinical strength antiperspirants are over-the-counter antiperspirants sold with higher concentrations of aluminium salts than ordinary products, aimed at people with heavy underarm sweating.[1] People use them to keep underarms dry, avoid visible sweat patches on shirts and keep odour down, which makes clothes sit and look cleaner through the day.[1][2]

Ordinary antiperspirants use aluminium salts to form temporary plugs in sweat ducts, and topical antiperspirants are listed as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis in guidelines.[1][2] Treatment with stronger aluminium chloride products is described as taking about three to five days to show improvement, with skin irritation as the most common side effect.[2]
Members of T Nation have discussed clinical strength products from several brands in threads on underarm sweating.[3][4] Evidence specific to branded clinical strength products was not located.

paras: The term is a marketing category rather than a regulatory one. The higher strength is intended for excessive sweating of the underarms, and for hands and feet in some cases.[2]

Skin irritation is the most commonly reported side effect of stronger aluminium chloride products.[2] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[1]

Alternatives described include topical glycopyrronium tosylate (FDA approved 2018 for underarm sweating), oral anticholinergics, botulinum toxin injections, microwave therapy, iontophoresis and surgery.[2]
No studies found specific to branded clinical strength antiperspirants. Wikipedia refers to evidence-based reviews of nonsurgical hyperhidrosis management.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation, clinical strength antiperspirants come up in threads by men looking for ways to stay dry.[3][4]

claims.claim: Clinical strength products cut underarm sweat
claims.believers: A 2008 poster said Gillette clinical strength cut way down on sweating in his underarms, though he said it worked 'kind of'.[4]
claims.experts: Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis; no studies specific to branded clinical strength products were located.[1][2]

claims.claim: Blocking underarm sweat moves sweating to other body areas
claims.believers: A 2009 poster wrote that with clinical strength products his underarms were dry but sweating shifted to other parts of his body.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were located on compensatory sweating from antiperspirant use.

card.note: Irritation is the most common side effect.

quick.overview:
Clinical strength antiperspirants contain more aluminium salt than regular ones and target heavy sweating.

Sources found on branded products are thin.
quick.mechanism: Aluminium salts plug sweat ducts so less sweat reaches the skin.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is the most common effect. People with kidney dysfunction are advised by the FDA to consult a doctor first.

chain: Higher-strength aluminium salts plug sweat ducts
Less underarm sweat reaches the skin and clothing
Dry underarms and no visible sweat marks on shirts
angle.text: The product is applied to underarms to reduce sweat output so shirts stay dry and odour is lower. It is used by people whose ordinary antiperspirant does not keep up.

infobox: About three to five days of use[2]
